subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which hormone increases water permeability of collecting ducts?

rationales.whyCorrect: ADH promotes insertion of aquaporin channels in collecting-duct cells.
rationales.eli10: ADH opens water doors so the kidney can save water.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which structure funnels urine into the ureter?

rationales.whyCorrect: The renal pelvis collects urine from calyces and narrows into the ureter.
rationales.eli10: It is a kidney funnel leading to the urine pipe.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Blood pressure falls. Which kidney enzyme begins the RAAS response?

rationales.whyCorrect: Juxtaglomerular cells release renin when perfusion or sodium delivery falls.
rationales.eli10: The kidney starts a chain of messages when blood pressure is too low.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Aldosterone acts on distal nephron cells. What changes?

options.text: Sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion rise

rationales.whyCorrect: Aldosterone increases sodium channels and sodium-potassium pumps.
rationales.eli10: The kidney saves more sodium while sending more potassium into urine.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which loop segment is water-permeable but relatively salt-impermeable?

rationales.whyCorrect: Water exits the descending limb into the hyperosmotic medulla.
rationales.eli10: This loop side lets water out but keeps most salt inside.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which loop segment helps create the medullary gradient by reabsorbing salt but not water?

rationales.whyCorrect: Salt transport without water dilutes tubular fluid and builds medullary osmolarity.
rationales.eli10: This side pumps salt out while water cannot follow.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: ADH rises during dehydration. What happens to urine?

rationales.whyCorrect: More collecting-duct water reabsorption conserves water and concentrates remaining solutes.
rationales.eli10: The kidney saves water, making less but darker urine.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Large plasma proteins normally stay in blood during filtration. Why?

options.text: The filtration barrier restricts size and charge

rationales.whyCorrect: Endothelium, basement membrane, and filtration slits exclude most proteins.
rationales.eli10: The filter's holes and electrical properties keep big proteins in blood.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: The proximal tubule cannot reabsorb glucose. What appears in urine?

rationales.whyCorrect: Filtered glucose remains in tubular fluid if its transport back to blood fails.
rationales.eli10: Sugar stays in the waste stream when its return doorway fails.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is tubular secretion useful for?

options.text: Adding selected wastes and ions from blood to filtrate
Moving urine from bladder to kidney

rationales.whyCorrect: Secretion helps eliminate drugs, acids, potassium, and metabolic wastes.
rationales.eli10: Tubule cells toss extra unwanted items into the urine stream.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which structure stores urine before elimination?

rationales.whyCorrect: The distensible muscular bladder temporarily holds urine.
rationales.eli10: The bladder is a stretchy storage bag for urine.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why can reduced kidney function cause nitrogenous wastes to rise in blood?

rationales.whyCorrect: Kidneys normally clear urea, creatinine, and other wastes from plasma.
rationales.eli10: If the filters work poorly, trash builds up in the blood.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Constriction of the afferent arteriole generally has what effect on filtration?

options.text: It decreases glomerular pressure and filtration

rationales.whyCorrect: Less blood enters glomerular capillaries, lowering filtration pressure.
rationales.eli10: Narrowing the incoming pipe reduces the push through the filter.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: How do kidneys help regulate acid-base balance?

options.text: They secrete hydrogen ions and manage bicarbonate
They convert all acids to proteins

rationales.whyCorrect: Renal tubules excrete acid and reabsorb or generate bicarbonate.
rationales.eli10: Kidneys remove acid and save an important base buffer.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What moves urine from the bladder to outside?

rationales.whyCorrect: The urethra is the final urinary passage.
rationales.eli10: The urethra is the body's exit tube for urine.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why does glucose in tubular fluid increase urine volume?

rationales.whyCorrect: Osmotic diuresis reduces water reabsorption from the nephron.
rationales.eli10: Sugar left in urine pulls water along with it.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Angiotensin II helps restore pressure through which effects?

rationales.whyCorrect: It raises resistance and promotes sodium and water retention.
rationales.eli10: It tightens blood pipes and tells kidneys to save salt and water.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: The medullary osmotic gradient is lost. Which renal ability declines most?

rationales.whyCorrect: ADH can reabsorb large amounts of water only when the medulla provides an osmotic pull.
rationales.eli10: Water doors help only if the surrounding tissue can pull water through them.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Filtration pressure falls, but GFR stays near normal briefly. What response can explain this?

rationales.whyCorrect: These adjustments help maintain glomerular capillary pressure.
rationales.eli10: Opening the entrance and narrowing the exit keeps pressure in the filter.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Plasma protein enters Bowman's space after barrier damage. What effect favors more filtration?

rationales.whyCorrect: Protein in filtrate osmotically attracts water across the damaged barrier.
rationales.eli10: Protein on the urine side acts like a water magnet pulling outward.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: ADH is high, but collecting-duct cells lack functional aquaporins. What happens?

options.text: Water reabsorption remains low despite the signal

rationales.whyCorrect: A hormone cannot produce its effect when the required response machinery fails.
rationales.eli10: The save-water message arrives, but the water doors are broken.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why can severe kidney failure disrupt nerves and muscles?

options.text: Potassium and acid-base balance may become abnormal

rationales.whyCorrect: Membrane excitability depends strongly on extracellular potassium and pH.
rationales.eli10: Bad salt and acid levels disturb the electricity used by nerves and muscles.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why does a substance's excretion rate equal filtration plus secretion minus reabsorption?

options.text: These are the three ways it enters or leaves tubular fluid

rationales.whyCorrect: Filtration and secretion add substance to the tubule; reabsorption removes it.
rationales.eli10: What leaves equals what entered the waste stream minus what the body took back.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which compartment contains most body water?

rationales.whyCorrect: Roughly two-thirds of body water lies inside cells.
rationales.eli10: Most body water is stored inside the body's many cells.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which ion is the major extracellular cation?

rationales.whyCorrect: Sodium is the dominant positive ion in extracellular fluid.
rationales.eli10: Sodium is the most common positive salt particle outside cells.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which ion is the major intracellular cation?

rationales.whyCorrect: Cells maintain high internal potassium through membrane transport.
rationales.eli10: Potassium is the main positive salt particle inside cells.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which chemical system resists sudden pH changes?

rationales.whyCorrect: Buffers accept or release hydrogen ions to limit pH shifts.
rationales.eli10: A buffer is a shock absorber for acids and bases.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Where are sperm produced?

rationales.whyCorrect: Spermatogenesis occurs in the seminiferous epithelium of testes.
rationales.eli10: Tiny coiled tubes inside the testes make sperm cells.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Where do sperm mature and gain motility?

rationales.whyCorrect: Sperm mature while passing through the coiled epididymal duct.
rationales.eli10: The epididymis is a training and storage tube for sperm.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which organ produces oocytes and ovarian hormones?

rationales.whyCorrect: Ovaries contain follicles and secrete estrogens and progesterone.
rationales.eli10: Ovaries hold developing egg cells and make reproductive hormones.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Where does implantation normally occur?

rationales.whyCorrect: The blastocyst normally attaches to and invades the uterine lining.
rationales.eli10: The early embryo settles into the soft inner lining of the uterus.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What does fertilization normally produce?

rationales.whyCorrect: Fusion of sperm and secondary oocyte produces a diploid zygote.
rationales.eli10: The first new cell forms when sperm and egg join.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A cell is placed in a hypertonic extracellular solution. What happens?

options.text: It gains sodium only with no water movement

rationales.whyCorrect: Water moves toward the higher nonpenetrating-solute concentration outside.
rationales.eli10: Water leaves the cell for the more crowded solution.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which condition can directly cause edema?

rationales.whyCorrect: Blocked drainage allows interstitial fluid and protein to accumulate.
rationales.eli10: A clogged tissue drain causes swelling.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Prolonged vomiting commonly causes which primary acid-base disturbance?

rationales.whyCorrect: Loss of hydrogen-rich gastric fluid raises body-fluid pH.
rationales.eli10: Losing too much stomach acid makes the body too basic.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Hypoventilation causes which disturbance?

rationales.whyCorrect: Retained carbon dioxide increases carbonic acid.
rationales.eli10: Breathing too little traps an acid-making gas.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Hyperventilation causes which primary disturbance?

rationales.whyCorrect: Excessive CO2 loss reduces carbonic acid and raises pH.
rationales.eli10: Breathing too fast blows away too much acid-making gas.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Severe diarrhea with bicarbonate loss can cause what?

rationales.whyCorrect: Loss of a major base lowers blood pH.
rationales.eli10: Losing too much base leaves body fluids more acidic.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Which hormone surge triggers ovulation?

rationales.whyCorrect: The midcycle luteinizing-hormone surge causes follicular rupture and oocyte release.
rationales.eli10: A sudden LH message tells the ovary to release the egg cell.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What does FSH support in the ovary?

rationales.whyCorrect: FSH promotes growth of ovarian follicles and estrogen production.
rationales.eli10: FSH helps an egg's tiny ovarian home grow and develop.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: After ovulation, which structure secretes much progesterone?

rationales.whyCorrect: The ruptured follicle becomes the progesterone-secreting corpus luteum.
rationales.eli10: The empty follicle changes into a temporary hormone factory.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: What is progesterone's major uterine effect after ovulation?

rationales.whyCorrect: Progesterone supports a nutrient-rich lining suited for implantation.
rationales.eli10: Progesterone keeps the uterus lining soft and ready.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Where does fertilization most commonly occur?

rationales.whyCorrect: Sperm commonly meets the oocyte in the widened ampulla.
rationales.eli10: Sperm and egg usually meet in the wide part of the tube.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Testosterone production in testes is stimulated mainly by what?

rationales.whyCorrect: LH stimulates interstitial Leydig cells to synthesize testosterone.
rationales.eli10: LH tells special testis cells to make testosterone.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why is meiosis necessary in gamete production?

rationales.whyCorrect: Haploid sperm and oocyte combine to restore the diploid number at fertilization.
rationales.eli10: Each parent gives half a chromosome set so the baby gets one full set.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Dehydration raises extracellular osmolarity. What happens to cells initially?

rationales.whyCorrect: Water shifts from intracellular to more concentrated extracellular fluid.
rationales.eli10: Water moves out of cells toward the saltier outside fluid.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why is potassium imbalance especially dangerous for the heart?

rationales.whyCorrect: Abnormal extracellular potassium can disrupt cardiac action potentials and rhythm.
rationales.eli10: Wrong potassium levels disturb the heart's electrical signals.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Plasma becomes hypotonic. Which shift occurs before regulation corrects it?

rationales.whyCorrect: Water moves toward the higher effective solute concentration inside cells.
rationales.eli10: Water flows into the more crowded cells and puffs them up.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: In respiratory acidosis, how do kidneys compensate over time?

options.text: Excrete more hydrogen and retain more bicarbonate

rationales.whyCorrect: Renal compensation increases base availability and removes acid.
rationales.eli10: Kidneys dump more acid and save more base to help balance blood.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: During metabolic acidosis, what rapid respiratory compensation occurs?

rationales.whyCorrect: Lowering CO2 reduces carbonic acid and raises pH toward normal.
rationales.eli10: Faster breathing blows away an acid-making gas.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: The corpus luteum degenerates without pregnancy. What triggers menstruation?

rationales.whyCorrect: Hormone withdrawal causes spiral-artery changes and shedding of functional endometrium.
rationales.eli10: When support hormones drop, the uterus releases the lining it built.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Why does hCG support early pregnancy?

options.text: It maintains the corpus luteum and progesterone secretion
It blocks all embryonic cell division

rationales.whyCorrect: Embryonic hCG preserves luteal support until the placenta produces sufficient hormones.
rationales.eli10: The early embryo sends a “keep the lining” message to the ovary.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A person loses isotonic extracellular fluid. What is the initial compartment change?

options.text: Extracellular volume decreases with little osmotic cell shift

rationales.whyCorrect: Because osmolarity is unchanged, little water shifts across cell membranes initially.
rationales.eli10: Outside-cell fluid shrinks, but equal saltiness gives water little reason to enter or leave cells.
